CHAPTER 32 - HEALTH AND HYGIENE

Introduction

Good health is one of the most valuable assets a person can have. A healthy individual is able to work, learn, play and contribute to society. This chapter explains what health and hygiene really mean, describes the different types of diseases and the agents that cause infectious diseases, examines how diseases spread and how they can be prevented, introduces immunity and vaccination, and discusses non-communicable and deficiency diseases, balanced diet, the dangers of addiction, and the basics of first aid.

32.1 MEANING OF HEALTH AND HYGIENE

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines HEALTH as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. This definition makes three important points. (1) PHYSICAL well-being means the body works properly - organs function normally, the person has energy and is free from illness. (2) MENTAL well-being means a balanced state of mind - the person can think clearly, handle stress, and feel emotionally stable. (3) SOCIAL well-being means the person can form good relationships and live in harmony with family, friends and community. Health is therefore much more than simply 'not being sick'.

HYGIENE refers to the practices and conditions that help maintain health and prevent the spread of disease. Hygiene has two parts. PERSONAL HYGIENE includes habits such as bathing daily, washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet, brushing teeth twice a day, keeping nails short and clean, wearing clean clothes, and getting enough sleep and exercise. COMMUNITY or PUBLIC HYGIENE includes the cleanliness of our surroundings - safe disposal of garbage and sewage, supply of clean drinking water, control of mosquitoes and flies, clean markets and food, and proper drainage. Both personal and community hygiene are needed because an individual cannot stay healthy in dirty surroundings, and clean surroundings are wasted if personal habits are poor.

32.2 WHAT IS A DISEASE?

A DISEASE is any condition that disturbs the normal functioning of the body or mind. When a person is diseased, one or more organs or systems do not work properly, and the person shows SYMPTOMS such as fever, pain, weakness, cough or rashes. Diseases can be classified in several ways.

By origin, diseases are either CONGENITAL or ACQUIRED. CONGENITAL diseases are present from birth; they are caused by genetic defects or by problems during the development of the baby in the womb. Examples are colour blindness, haemophilia, Down syndrome and a hole in the heart. ACQUIRED diseases develop after birth, during the course of a person's life, due to infection, poor diet, lifestyle or injury.

Acquired diseases are further divided into COMMUNICABLE (infectious) and NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases. COMMUNICABLE diseases are caused by germs (pathogens) and can spread from a sick person to a healthy person. NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases do not spread from person to person; they are usually caused by lifestyle, ageing, deficiency of nutrients, or malfunction of body organs.

32.3 INFECTIOUS DISEASES AND THEIR AGENTS

Infectious (communicable) diseases are caused by tiny living organisms called PATHOGENS or disease-causing agents. The main groups of pathogens are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and worms (helminths).

BACTERIA are single-celled microorganisms. Harmful bacteria cause diseases such as TUBERCULOSIS (caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, affecting the lungs), CHOLERA (caused by Vibrio cholerae, causing severe watery diarrhoea), TYPHOID (caused by Salmonella typhi), tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough. Bacterial diseases can often be treated with ANTIBIOTICS.

VIRUSES are extremely small agents that can multiply only inside living cells. Viral diseases include the COMMON COLD, INFLUENZA (flu), COVID-19, DENGUE, POLIO, measles, mumps, chickenpox, hepatitis, rabies and AIDS (caused by HIV, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus). Antibiotics do NOT work against viruses; many viral diseases are prevented by vaccination.

FUNGI are organisms that can cause skin infections. RINGWORM (a fungal infection of the skin that forms ring-shaped patches) and athlete's foot are common examples. Fungal infections spread in warm, moist, unclean conditions.

PROTOZOA are single-celled animal-like organisms. MALARIA is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, which is spread by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. AMOEBIASIS (amoebic dysentery), caused by Entamoeba histolytica, affects the intestine and spreads through contaminated food and water.

WORMS (helminths) are parasites that live inside the body. ASCARIASIS is caused by the roundworm Ascaris, which lives in the intestine and spreads through food and water contaminated with worm eggs. Tapeworm and hookworm are other worm infections.

32.4 MODES OF TRANSMISSION OF DISEASES

Infectious diseases spread from a sick person (or carrier) to a healthy person in several ways.
 - AIR-BORNE: germs travel in tiny droplets released when a sick person coughs, sneezes or talks. Examples: common cold, influenza, tuberculosis, COVID-19, measles.
 - WATER-BORNE: germs spread through contaminated drinking water. Examples: cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, amoebiasis.
 - FOOD-BORNE: germs spread through contaminated or stale food. Examples: typhoid, food poisoning, amoebiasis.
 - VECTOR-BORNE: an animal (a vector), usually an insect, carries the germ from one person to another. The female Anopheles mosquito spreads malaria; the Aedes mosquito spreads dengue; the housefly carries germs of cholera and typhoid onto food.
 - CONTACT: germs spread by touching an infected person or contaminated objects, or through body fluids. Examples: ringworm and skin infections (direct touch); AIDS and hepatitis B (through blood, unsafe sex or shared needles).

32.5 PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES

Infectious diseases can be prevented by breaking the chain of transmission:
 - Maintain personal hygiene - wash hands frequently with soap, bathe regularly.
 - Drink only clean, boiled or filtered water; eat freshly cooked, covered food.
 - Cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing; wear a mask during outbreaks; keep a safe distance from sick people.
 - Control vectors - prevent water from collecting (where mosquitoes breed), use mosquito nets and repellents, keep surroundings clean to reduce flies.
 - Dispose of garbage and sewage safely; keep food and water sources clean.
 - Get vaccinated against preventable diseases and complete the full course of any prescribed medicine.

32.6 IMMUNITY

IMMUNITY is the ability of the body to resist and fight disease-causing germs. There are two main types.
INNATE (natural) immunity is present from birth. It includes general defences such as the skin (a physical barrier), tears and saliva (which contain germ-killing substances), the acid in the stomach, and white blood cells that engulf and destroy germs. Innate immunity acts against many germs in a general way.
ACQUIRED immunity develops during a person's life. When a germ enters the body, special white blood cells recognise it and produce proteins called ANTIBODIES that attack and neutralise that particular germ. After recovery, the body 'remembers' the germ, so if the same germ enters again, antibodies are made quickly and the person does not fall ill. Acquired immunity can also be gained through vaccination.

32.7 VACCINATION AND IMMUNISATION

A VACCINE contains dead or weakened germs (or parts of germs) that cannot cause the disease but can train the body's immune system. When a vaccine is given, the body produces antibodies and 'memory' cells against that germ. If the real germ later enters the body, the immune system destroys it quickly and the person is protected. The process of giving vaccines to protect against disease is called IMMUNISATION or vaccination. Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine (against smallpox). In India, the NATIONAL IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME (Universal Immunisation Programme) gives free vaccines to infants and children against diseases such as tuberculosis (BCG), polio (OPV), diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus (DPT), measles and hepatitis B. Thanks to vaccination, smallpox has been completely eradicated worldwide and polio has been eliminated from India.

32.8 NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES AND LIFESTYLE

NON-COMMUNICABLE diseases do not spread from person to person. They are often called LIFESTYLE diseases because they are linked to how we live - diet, exercise, stress and habits.
 - DIABETES: the body cannot control the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood, because of a problem with the hormone insulin. Blood sugar rises too high.
 - HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure): blood pushes too hard against the walls of blood vessels, which can damage the heart, kidneys and brain.
 - HEART DISEASE: the blood vessels supplying the heart may become narrow or blocked, which can cause a heart attack. Risk factors include a fatty diet, smoking, obesity and lack of exercise.
 - CANCER: certain body cells divide in an uncontrolled way and form lumps called tumours. Tobacco, certain chemicals and radiation increase the risk of cancer.
These diseases can largely be prevented by a balanced diet, regular exercise, maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and managing stress.

32.9 DEFICIENCY DISEASES

DEFICIENCY diseases are caused by a lack (deficiency) of one or more nutrients - vitamins, minerals or proteins - in the diet. They are non-communicable. Important examples:
 - SCURVY: deficiency of vitamin C; symptoms are bleeding and swollen gums. Prevented by citrus fruits (amla, lemon, orange).
 - RICKETS: deficiency of vitamin D (and calcium); causes soft, bent bones in children. Prevented by sunlight, milk and a balanced diet.
 - BERI-BERI: deficiency of vitamin B1 (thiamine); affects the nerves and muscles.
 - ANAEMIA: deficiency of iron; the blood has too little haemoglobin, so the person feels weak and tired. Prevented by iron-rich foods such as green leafy vegetables and jaggery.
 - GOITRE: deficiency of iodine; the thyroid gland in the neck swells. Prevented by using iodised salt.
 - NIGHT BLINDNESS: deficiency of vitamin A; the person cannot see well in dim light.

32.10 BALANCED DIET AND NUTRITION

A BALANCED DIET is one that contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage (fibre) - in the right amounts. CARBOHYDRATES and FATS give energy; PROTEINS build and repair the body; VITAMINS and MINERALS keep the body working properly and protect against deficiency diseases; WATER and ROUGHAGE help digestion and remove waste. The right diet depends on a person's age, sex and activity. A balanced diet, along with clean food and water, is the foundation of good health.

32.11 ADDICTION AND ABUSE

ADDICTION is a strong, harmful dependence on a substance, so that a person finds it very hard to stop using it even when it damages their health. The commonly abused substances are tobacco, alcohol and drugs.
 - TOBACCO (in cigarettes, bidis, gutkha): contains nicotine. It damages the lungs and heart and causes cancer of the mouth and lungs.
 - ALCOHOL: damages the liver (cirrhosis), brain and stomach, and leads to accidents and family problems.
 - DRUGS (such as opium, heroin, cannabis): damage the brain and nervous system, spread infections like AIDS through shared needles, and destroy a person's studies, work and family life.
All these substances harm the body, the mind and society. The best protection is to never start, to say no to peer pressure, and to seek help (counselling, de-addiction centres) for someone who is already addicted.

32.12 FIRST AID

FIRST AID is the immediate, temporary help given to an injured or suddenly ill person before a doctor or hospital can be reached. Its aims are to save life, prevent the condition from getting worse, and help recovery. Basic first aid includes:
 - CUTS AND WOUNDS: wash with clean water, press a clean cloth to stop bleeding, and cover with a clean bandage.
 - BURNS: cool the burnt area with clean running water; do not apply ice, oil or toothpaste; cover loosely.
 - FRACTURE (broken bone): keep the part still using a splint and take the person to hospital.
 - FAINTING: lay the person flat, loosen tight clothing and give fresh air.
A simple first-aid box should contain clean bandages, cotton, antiseptic, scissors and a pain reliever. First aid is not a substitute for proper medical treatment - always get a doctor's help for serious injuries.

SUMMARY

- Health (WHO) is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease. Hygiene (personal + community) keeps us healthy.
- Diseases are congenital (from birth) or acquired (later). Acquired diseases are communicable (infectious) or non-communicable.
- Infectious diseases are caused by bacteria (TB, cholera, typhoid), viruses (cold, flu, COVID-19, dengue, polio, AIDS), fungi (ringworm), protozoa (malaria, amoebiasis) and worms (ascariasis).
- Diseases spread through air, water, food, vectors and contact; they are prevented by hygiene, clean water and food, vector control and vaccination.
- Immunity is innate (from birth) or acquired (antibodies). Vaccination trains the immune system; India's national immunisation programme protects children.
- Non-communicable diseases (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer) are linked to lifestyle. Deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, beri-beri, anaemia, goitre) come from a poor diet.
- A balanced diet, avoiding addiction (tobacco, alcohol, drugs), and knowing basic first aid all support good health.

topics.name: Health, Hygiene and Disease
topics.description: The WHO definition of health (physical, mental, social well-being); personal and community hygiene; what a disease is; and the classification of diseases (congenital vs acquired, communicable vs non-communicable).

topics.description: Infectious diseases and the five groups of pathogens that cause them - bacteria (TB, cholera, typhoid), viruses (cold, flu, COVID-19, dengue, polio, AIDS), fungi (ringworm), protozoa (malaria, amoebiasis) and worms (ascariasis).

topics.name: Transmission and Prevention of Diseases
topics.description: How infectious diseases are transmitted - through air, water, food, vectors (mosquitoes, flies) and contact - and the measures used to prevent and control their spread.

topics.description: Non-communicable lifestyle diseases (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer) and deficiency diseases caused by a lack of vitamins or minerals (scurvy, rickets, beri-beri, anaemia, goitre).

topics.name: Balanced Diet, Addiction and First Aid
topics.description: The components of a balanced diet and their roles; the harmful effects of addiction to tobacco, alcohol and drugs; and the basics of first aid for common emergencies.

chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 32 explains the meaning of health and hygiene, the types of diseases and the agents of infectious disease, how diseases spread and are prevented, immunity and vaccination, and the role of diet, addiction and first aid in keeping people healthy.

sections.heading: Health, hygiene and disease
bullets: WHO defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being - not merely the absence of disease.
Personal hygiene (bathing, hand-washing, brushing teeth, clean clothes) and community hygiene (clean water, garbage and sewage disposal, vector control) together protect health.
A disease is any disturbance of the normal functioning of the body or mind, shown by symptoms such as fever, pain or weakness.
Diseases are congenital (present from birth) or acquired (developed later); acquired diseases are communicable (infectious) or non-communicable.

sections.heading: Infectious diseases and their agents
bullets: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and worms.
Bacterial: tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid (often treated with antibiotics). Viral: common cold, influenza, COVID-19, dengue, polio, AIDS (antibiotics do not work).
Fungal: ringworm. Protozoan: malaria (Plasmodium), amoebiasis. Worm: ascariasis (roundworm).

sections.heading: Transmission and prevention
bullets: Diseases spread through air (cold, TB, COVID-19), water (cholera, typhoid), food, vectors (mosquito - malaria, dengue; housefly) and contact (ringworm, AIDS).
Prevention: personal hygiene and hand-washing, clean boiled water and fresh food, covering coughs and wearing masks.
Control also means destroying vectors and their breeding sites, safe waste disposal and completing prescribed medicine.

sections.heading: Immunity and vaccination
bullets: Immunity is the body's ability to resist germs; it is innate (present from birth - skin, stomach acid, white blood cells) or acquired (during life).
Acquired immunity works through antibodies - proteins made by white blood cells that neutralise a specific germ, and the body remembers it afterwards.
A vaccine contains dead or weakened germs that train the immune system; India's National Immunisation Programme gives free vaccines (BCG, OPV, DPT, measles, hepatitis B) to children.

sections.heading: Lifestyle diseases, deficiency, diet and first aid
bullets: Non-communicable lifestyle diseases include diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and cancer; they are prevented by good diet, exercise and avoiding tobacco.
Deficiency diseases: scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D), beri-beri (vitamin B1), anaemia (iron), goitre (iodine).

A balanced diet supplies carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage; addiction to tobacco, alcohol and drugs harms health; first aid gives immediate help before a doctor is reached.

key_takeaways: Health (WHO) is complete physical, mental and social well-being; personal and community hygiene maintain it.
Diseases are congenital or acquired; acquired diseases are communicable (infectious) or non-communicable.
Infectious diseases are caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and worms, each with characteristic diseases.
Diseases spread by air, water, food, vectors and contact, and are prevented by hygiene, clean food/water, vector control and vaccination.
Immunity is innate or acquired; antibodies fight germs, and vaccines train the immune system to give protection.

Non-communicable lifestyle diseases (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer) and deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, beri-beri, anaemia, goitre) are largely prevented by a balanced diet and healthy living.
A balanced diet, avoidance of addiction, and knowledge of basic first aid together support lifelong good health.

glossary.definition: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO definition).
Practices and conditions - personal and community - that help maintain health and prevent the spread of disease.
Any condition that disturbs the normal functioning of the body or mind, usually shown by symptoms.
A disease present from birth, caused by a genetic defect or by problems during development in the womb (e.g. colour blindness).
An infectious disease caused by pathogens that can spread from a sick person to a healthy person.
A disease that does not spread from person to person; caused by lifestyle, ageing or nutrient deficiency.
A disease-causing organism such as a bacterium, virus, fungus, protozoan or worm.
An animal, usually an insect, that carries a pathogen from one host to another (e.g. the Anopheles mosquito carries malaria).
The ability of the body to resist and fight disease-causing germs; it may be innate or acquired.
A protein made by white blood cells that recognises and neutralises a specific germ in the body.
A preparation of dead or weakened germs that trains the immune system to protect against a disease without causing it.
The process of giving vaccines to protect a person against infectious diseases; also called vaccination.
A disease caused by a lack of a nutrient (vitamin, mineral or protein) in the diet, e.g. scurvy or anaemia.
A diet that contains all nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the right amounts.
The immediate, temporary help given to an injured or suddenly ill person before a doctor or hospital is reached.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Health and Hygiene (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-32 for Lesson 32. Attempt all questions. Answer in your own words and give examples where asked.

questions.question: State the WHO definition of health and name its three dimensions.
questions.answer: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. Its three dimensions are: (1) PHYSICAL well-being - the body works properly and is free from illness; (2) MENTAL well-being - a balanced, stable state of mind able to handle stress; (3) SOCIAL well-being - good relationships and harmony with family and community.
questions.explanation: Recall the WHO definition and its three components.

questions.question: Differentiate between personal hygiene and community (public) hygiene with two examples each.
questions.answer: PERSONAL hygiene is the set of habits an individual practises to stay clean and healthy - examples: bathing daily and washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet; brushing teeth twice a day and wearing clean clothes. COMMUNITY (public) hygiene is the cleanliness of the surroundings shared by everyone - examples: safe disposal of garbage and sewage; supply of clean drinking water and control of mosquitoes and flies. Both are needed: an individual cannot stay healthy in dirty surroundings, and clean surroundings are wasted if personal habits are poor.
questions.explanation: Personal = individual habits; community = surroundings; two examples each.

questions.question: Distinguish between congenital and acquired diseases with one example of each.
questions.answer: CONGENITAL diseases are present from birth and are caused by genetic defects or problems during development in the womb - example: colour blindness (or haemophilia, Down syndrome). ACQUIRED diseases develop after birth during the course of life, due to infection, poor diet, lifestyle or injury - example: cholera (or tuberculosis, diabetes). In short, congenital = present at birth; acquired = developed later.
questions.explanation: Congenital from birth; acquired developed later. One example each.

questions.question: Name the five groups of pathogens that cause infectious diseases and give one disease caused by each.
questions.answer: (1) BACTERIA - tuberculosis (or cholera, typhoid). (2) VIRUSES - common cold (or influenza, COVID-19, dengue, polio, AIDS). (3) FUNGI - ringworm. (4) PROTOZOA - malaria (or amoebiasis). (5) WORMS (helminths) - ascariasis. These five groups of disease-causing organisms are called pathogens.
questions.explanation: Bacteria, virus, fungi, protozoa, worms - one disease each.

questions.question: Describe the five modes of transmission of infectious diseases, giving one example disease for each.
questions.answer:
Infectious diseases spread from a sick person (or carrier) to a healthy person in five main ways:
(1) AIR-BORNE - germs travel in droplets released when a sick person coughs or sneezes; example: common cold, influenza, tuberculosis, COVID-19.
(2) WATER-BORNE - germs spread through contaminated drinking water; example: cholera, typhoid.
(3) FOOD-BORNE - germs spread through contaminated or stale food; example: typhoid, amoebiasis, food poisoning.
(4) VECTOR-BORNE - an insect carries the germ; example: the female Anopheles mosquito spreads malaria, the Aedes mosquito spreads dengue, the housefly carries cholera germs.
(5) CONTACT - germs spread by touching an infected person or contaminated objects, or through body fluids; example: ringworm (touch), AIDS (blood/needles).
questions.explanation: Air, water, food, vector, contact - with an example each.

questions.question: List four measures that can prevent and control the spread of infectious diseases.
questions.answer: (1) Maintain personal hygiene - wash hands with soap and bathe regularly. (2) Drink only clean, boiled or filtered water and eat freshly cooked, covered food. (3) Cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing, wear a mask during outbreaks and keep a distance from sick people. (4) Control vectors - prevent water from collecting, use mosquito nets, keep surroundings clean - and get vaccinated against preventable diseases. These measures break the chain of transmission.
questions.explanation: Hygiene, clean water/food, covering coughs, vector control and vaccination.

questions.question: Differentiate between innate and acquired immunity.
questions.answer: INNATE (natural) immunity is present from birth and acts in a general way against many germs. It includes the skin (a barrier), tears and saliva, the acid in the stomach, and white blood cells that engulf germs. ACQUIRED immunity develops during life: when a germ enters, white blood cells make ANTIBODIES against that particular germ, and the body remembers it so it can respond quickly next time. Acquired immunity can also be gained through vaccination. In short: innate = present at birth and general; acquired = developed during life and germ-specific.
questions.explanation: Innate present at birth and general; acquired developed during life and specific (antibodies).

questions.question: What is a vaccine? Explain briefly how vaccination protects a person from disease.
questions.answer: A VACCINE contains dead or weakened germs (or parts of germs) that cannot cause the disease but can train the immune system. When the vaccine is given, the body produces ANTIBODIES and 'memory' cells against that germ. If the real germ later enters the body, the immune system recognises and destroys it quickly, so the person does not fall ill. This is how vaccination (immunisation) gives protection; India's National Immunisation Programme uses vaccines such as BCG, OPV, DPT, measles and hepatitis B.
questions.explanation: Vaccine = dead/weakened germs; it triggers antibodies and memory, giving protection.

questions.question: Name the deficiency disease and the missing nutrient for each: (a) scurvy (b) rickets (c) anaemia (d) goitre.
questions.answer: (a) SCURVY - deficiency of vitamin C (causes bleeding, swollen gums). (b) RICKETS - deficiency of vitamin D (and calcium), causing soft, bent bones in children. (c) ANAEMIA - deficiency of iron, causing low haemoglobin, weakness and tiredness. (d) GOITRE - deficiency of iodine, causing swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck (prevented by iodised salt).
questions.explanation: Scurvy = vitamin C; rickets = vitamin D; anaemia = iron; goitre = iodine.

questions.question: What is addiction? Describe the harmful effects of tobacco, alcohol and drugs, and suggest how addiction can be prevented.
questions.answer:
ADDICTION is a strong, harmful dependence on a substance, so that a person finds it very hard to stop using it even when it damages their health.
HARMFUL EFFECTS:
- TOBACCO (cigarettes, bidis, gutkha) contains nicotine; it damages the lungs and heart and causes cancer of the mouth and lungs.
- ALCOHOL damages the liver (cirrhosis), brain and stomach and leads to accidents and family problems.
- DRUGS (opium, heroin, cannabis) damage the brain and nervous system, can spread infections like AIDS through shared needles, and destroy a person's studies, work and family life.
PREVENTION: never start; say no to peer pressure; lead a healthy active life; and seek help through counselling and de-addiction centres for someone already addicted. All these substances harm the body, the mind and society.
questions.explanation: Define addiction; effects of tobacco, alcohol, drugs; prevention by avoidance and counselling.

questions.question: The WHO definition of health includes physical, mental and ____ well-being.
Bathing daily and washing hands are examples of ____ hygiene.
A disease present from birth is called a ____ disease.
Diseases that spread from a sick person to a healthy person are called ____ diseases.
Disease-causing organisms are called ____.
Ringworm is caused by a ____.
AIDS is caused by the ____ virus.
An insect that carries a pathogen from one person to another is called a ____.
Malaria is spread by the female ____ mosquito.
Proteins that neutralise specific germs in the body are called ____.
The vaccine that protects against tuberculosis is ____.
In diabetes, the body cannot control the level of ____ in the blood.
Scurvy is caused by the deficiency of vitamin ____.
Anaemia is caused by the deficiency of ____.
The immediate temporary help given to an injured person is called ____.
Define health as given by the WHO.
questions.answer: The WHO defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. It therefore covers the body, the mind and a person's social relationships, not just freedom from illness.

questions.question: Why is community hygiene as important as personal hygiene?
questions.answer: Personal hygiene keeps an individual clean, but a person cannot stay healthy in dirty surroundings. Community hygiene - clean drinking water, safe disposal of garbage and sewage, and control of mosquitoes and flies - removes the sources of germs in our shared environment. Both are needed together for good health.
questions.explanation: Both protect health; neither alone is enough.

questions.question: List four good personal-hygiene habits and explain how they protect health.
questions.answer: (1) Washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet removes germs before they enter the body. (2) Bathing daily keeps the skin clean and free of germs. (3) Brushing teeth twice a day prevents tooth decay and gum disease. (4) Wearing clean clothes and keeping nails short prevents skin and stomach infections. Together these habits break the chain by which germs reach us.

questions.question: Give two examples each of communicable and non-communicable diseases.
questions.answer: COMMUNICABLE (spread by germs): tuberculosis and cholera (also typhoid, influenza, COVID-19). NON-COMMUNICABLE (do not spread): diabetes and hypertension (also heart disease, cancer, scurvy).

questions.question: How are diseases classified? Draw the classification in words.
questions.answer: Diseases are first classified by origin into CONGENITAL (present from birth, e.g. colour blindness) and ACQUIRED (developed later in life). Acquired diseases are further divided into COMMUNICABLE (infectious, spread by pathogens, e.g. cholera) and NON-COMMUNICABLE (do not spread, e.g. diabetes, deficiency diseases). So the tree is: Disease -> Congenital / Acquired; Acquired -> Communicable / Non-communicable.
questions.explanation: Congenital vs acquired; acquired -> communicable vs non-communicable.

questions.question: What is a pathogen? Name the five groups of pathogens.
questions.answer: A PATHOGEN is a disease-causing organism. The five groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and worms (helminths).

questions.question: Name two bacterial and two viral diseases.
questions.answer: Bacterial: tuberculosis and cholera (also typhoid). Viral: common cold and influenza (also COVID-19, dengue, polio, AIDS).

questions.question: Match each pathogen group to one disease: bacteria, virus, fungus, protozoan, worm.
questions.answer: Bacteria - tuberculosis (or cholera/typhoid). Virus - common cold (or influenza, COVID-19, dengue, polio, AIDS). Fungus - ringworm. Protozoan - malaria (or amoebiasis). Worm - ascariasis. Each group of pathogens causes characteristic infectious diseases.

questions.question: Why do antibiotics not work against viral diseases?
questions.answer: Antibiotics act on structures and processes found in BACTERIA - for example, the bacterial cell wall and bacterial protein-making machinery. VIRUSES are not cells; they have a completely different structure and multiply inside our own cells, so antibiotics have nothing to act on. This is why viral diseases such as colds and influenza are not cured by antibiotics; many are instead prevented by vaccines.
questions.explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial structures, which viruses lack.

questions.question: What kind of disease is malaria and how is it caused?
questions.answer: Malaria is a protozoan disease caused by Plasmodium. The parasite is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito; when an infected mosquito bites a person, the parasite enters the blood and causes fever with chills.

questions.question: Name two diseases prevented by vaccination and the pathogen type of each.
questions.answer: Polio (viral) and tuberculosis (bacterial) are both prevented by vaccination (OPV and BCG). Measles (viral) and tetanus/diphtheria (bacterial) are other vaccine-preventable diseases.

questions.question: Name the five modes of transmission of infectious diseases.
questions.answer: The five modes are: (1) air-borne (droplets), (2) water-borne, (3) food-borne, (4) vector-borne (by insects such as mosquitoes and flies), and (5) contact (touch or body fluids).

questions.question: Explain, with examples, air-borne and water-borne transmission.
questions.answer: AIR-BORNE: germs travel in tiny droplets released when a sick person coughs, sneezes or talks, and a healthy person breathes them in. Examples: common cold, influenza, tuberculosis, COVID-19. WATER-BORNE: germs spread through drinking water contaminated with sewage or waste. Examples: cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A. The key difference is the medium - air versus contaminated water.
questions.explanation: Two routes with examples and difference.

questions.question: Suggest three ways to prevent mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue.
questions.answer: (1) Remove stagnant water from pots, coolers, tyres and drains so mosquitoes cannot breed. (2) Use mosquito nets, screens and repellents to avoid bites. (3) Keep surroundings clean and support community spraying/fogging. These measures control the mosquito vector and break the chain of transmission.

questions.question: How can we prevent water-borne diseases at home?
questions.answer: Drink only clean water that has been boiled or filtered, store it in covered clean containers, wash hands with soap before handling food, and eat freshly cooked covered food. Keeping the water source clean prevents cholera and typhoid.

questions.question: How does AIDS spread, and how is it NOT spread?
questions.answer: AIDS (caused by HIV) spreads through unsafe blood transfusion, sharing infected needles, unprotected sex, and from an infected mother to her baby. It does NOT spread through air, water, sharing food, or simply touching or sitting with an infected person.
questions.explanation: Contact through body fluids; not by casual contact.

questions.question: What is immunity? Name its two types.
questions.answer: Immunity is the ability of the body to resist and fight disease-causing germs. Its two types are innate (natural) immunity, present from birth, and acquired immunity, developed during life.

questions.question: Explain how acquired immunity protects the body using the idea of antibodies.
questions.answer: When a germ enters the body, special white blood cells recognise it and produce proteins called ANTIBODIES that attack and neutralise that particular germ, helping the person recover. The body then keeps 'memory' cells, so if the same germ enters again, antibodies are made very quickly and the person does not fall ill. This germ-specific, memory-based defence is acquired immunity.

questions.question: What is a vaccine and how does vaccination work?
questions.answer: A vaccine is a preparation of dead or weakened germs (or parts of germs) that cannot cause the disease. When given, it makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells against that germ. If the real germ later enters the body, the immune system destroys it quickly, so the person is protected. This process is called vaccination or immunisation.
questions.explanation: Vaccine trains the immune system to respond fast.

questions.question: What is the National Immunisation Programme? Name two vaccines it provides.
questions.answer: India's National (Universal) Immunisation Programme gives free vaccines to infants and children to protect them from serious diseases. Two of its vaccines are BCG (against tuberculosis) and OPV (oral polio vaccine, against polio); it also gives DPT, measles and hepatitis B vaccines.

questions.question: Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity with examples.
questions.answer: INNATE immunity is present from birth and acts generally against many germs - examples: the skin barrier, stomach acid, tears, and white blood cells that engulf germs. ACQUIRED immunity develops during life and is specific to a particular germ; it works through antibodies and memory cells (gained after an infection or by vaccination). So innate = general and inborn; acquired = specific and developed.

questions.question: What are lifestyle diseases? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Lifestyle (non-communicable) diseases are diseases linked to how we live - our diet, exercise, stress and habits - and they do not spread from person to person. Examples: diabetes and hypertension (also heart disease and cancer).

questions.question: What happens in diabetes and in hypertension?
questions.answer: In DIABETES the body cannot control the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood, because of a problem with the hormone insulin, so blood sugar rises too high. In HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure) the blood pushes too hard against the walls of the blood vessels, which can damage the heart, kidneys and brain.
questions.explanation: Diabetes = high blood sugar; hypertension = high blood pressure.

questions.question: Suggest three ways to prevent non-communicable lifestyle diseases.
questions.answer: (1) Eat a balanced diet with less salt, sugar and fat and more fruits and vegetables. (2) Exercise regularly and maintain a healthy body weight. (3) Avoid tobacco and alcohol and manage stress. These habits lower the risk of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and cancer.

questions.question: How is tobacco use linked to heart disease and cancer?
questions.answer: Tobacco contains nicotine and other harmful chemicals. It narrows and damages blood vessels, raising the risk of high blood pressure and heart attack, and its chemicals damage cells and cause cancer of the mouth and lungs. So tobacco is a major risk factor for both heart disease and cancer.
questions.explanation: Tobacco damages vessels and cells - heart disease and cancer.

questions.question: What are deficiency diseases? Give two examples with the missing nutrient.
questions.answer: Deficiency diseases are non-communicable diseases caused by a lack of a nutrient in the diet. Examples: scurvy (deficiency of vitamin C) and anaemia (deficiency of iron). Goitre (iodine) and rickets (vitamin D) are others.
questions.explanation: Caused by nutrient lack; two examples.

questions.question: Match the deficiency disease to its nutrient and one prevention: scurvy, rickets, goitre.
questions.answer: SCURVY - deficiency of vitamin C; prevented by citrus fruits (amla, lemon, orange). RICKETS - deficiency of vitamin D (and calcium); prevented by sunlight and milk. GOITRE - deficiency of iodine; prevented by using iodised salt.

questions.question: A person has weakness, tiredness and low haemoglobin. Which deficiency is likely and how can the diet be improved?
questions.answer: These are signs of ANAEMIA, caused by iron deficiency. The diet should include iron-rich foods such as green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates and pulses, which raise haemoglobin and relieve weakness.

questions.question: What is a balanced diet? Name the nutrients it should contain.
questions.answer: A balanced diet is one that contains all the nutrients in the right amounts: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage (fibre). It supplies energy, builds and repairs the body, and protects against deficiency diseases.

questions.question: State the correct first aid for (a) a small cut, (b) a minor burn, and (c) fainting.
questions.answer: (a) SMALL CUT: wash with clean water, press a clean cloth to stop bleeding, and cover with a clean bandage. (b) MINOR BURN: cool the area with clean running water, do not apply ice, oil or toothpaste, and cover loosely. (c) FAINTING: lay the person flat, loosen tight clothing and give plenty of fresh air. Seek a doctor's help for anything serious.
questions.explanation: First aid for cut, burn, fainting.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Ravi is not ill, but he often feels lonely, sleeps badly and is unable to concentrate. His friend says he is perfectly healthy because he has no disease.

(i) State the WHO definition of health.
(ii) Is Ravi fully healthy? Give a reason.
(iii) Which dimensions of health are affected in Ravi?
(iv) Suggest one habit that would improve his health.
questions.answer:
(i) The WHO defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'.
(ii) No. Although he has no disease, he is not in complete well-being, so he is not fully healthy.
(iii) His MENTAL well-being (poor sleep, poor concentration) and SOCIAL well-being (loneliness) are affected.
(iv) Regular exercise, a fixed sleep routine, or spending time with friends/family would improve his mental and social health.
questions.explanation: Health is more than absence of disease; mental and social dimensions matter.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a class, one student has colour blindness, another has cholera, a third has diabetes, and a fourth has the common cold.

(i) Which of these is a congenital disease?
(ii) Which are communicable diseases?
(iii) Which is a non-communicable acquired disease?
(iv) Define a communicable disease.
questions.answer:
(i) Colour blindness is congenital (present from birth).
(ii) Cholera and the common cold are communicable (infectious) diseases.
(iii) Diabetes is a non-communicable acquired disease.
(iv) A communicable disease is an infectious disease caused by pathogens that can spread from a sick person to a healthy person.
questions.explanation: Classify by origin and by whether they spread.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A doctor lists four diseases: tuberculosis, malaria, ringworm and the common cold.

(i) Which is caused by a bacterium?
(ii) Which is caused by a protozoan?
(iii) Which is a fungal disease?
(iv) Which is viral, and why will antibiotics not cure it?
questions.answer:
(i) Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium (Mycobacterium tuberculosis).
(ii) Malaria is caused by a protozoan (Plasmodium).
(iii) Ringworm is a fungal disease.
(iv) The common cold is viral; antibiotics will not cure it because antibiotics act on bacterial structures, which viruses do not have.
questions.explanation: Identify pathogen type; antibiotics only work on bacteria.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Viral diseases include the common cold, influenza, COVID-19, dengue, polio and AIDS.

(i) Name the virus that causes AIDS.
(ii) Which two of these are spread by mosquitoes or droplets respectively?
(iii) Name one viral disease prevented by vaccination.
(iv) Why are viral diseases generally harder to treat than bacterial ones?
questions.answer:
(i) AIDS is caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus).
(ii) Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito; the common cold/influenza/COVID-19 spread by droplets in the air.
(iii) Polio is prevented by vaccination (OPV); measles is another example.
(iv) Viruses multiply inside our own cells and are not affected by antibiotics, so there are few medicines that kill them - prevention by vaccination is the main approach.
questions.explanation: Viral diseases; HIV, transmission, vaccines, why hard to treat.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

After heavy rain, a village has stagnant water everywhere. Many people fall ill with malaria and dengue, and some get cholera.

(i) Which mode of transmission causes malaria and dengue here?
(ii) Which mode of transmission causes cholera?
(iii) Suggest two measures to control mosquitoes.
(iv) Suggest one measure to prevent cholera.
questions.answer:
(i) Malaria and dengue are VECTOR-BORNE - spread by mosquitoes (Anopheles for malaria, Aedes for dengue) that breed in the stagnant water.
(ii) Cholera is WATER-BORNE - spread by drinking water contaminated with germs.
(iii) Remove or drain stagnant water so mosquitoes cannot breed; use mosquito nets and repellents (and community spraying).
(iv) Drink only boiled or filtered water and keep the water source clean.
questions.explanation: Vector-borne vs water-borne; controls for each.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

During an outbreak of a respiratory illness, health workers advise people to wear masks, wash hands often and avoid crowds.

(i) By which mode does a respiratory illness mainly spread?
(ii) How does wearing a mask help?
(iii) How does hand-washing help?
(iv) Name one respiratory disease that spreads this way.
questions.answer:
(i) Mainly by the AIR-BORNE route - through droplets released when a sick person coughs, sneezes or talks.
(ii) A mask traps the droplets, so germs are not breathed out or in - it breaks the chain of transmission.
(iii) Hand-washing removes germs picked up from surfaces before they can reach the mouth, nose or eyes.
(iv) Influenza (flu), the common cold, COVID-19 or tuberculosis.
questions.explanation: Air-borne spread; masks and hand-washing break transmission.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A baby is given several vaccines, including BCG and OPV, in the first months of life under a government programme.

(i) Name the programme.
(ii) What does a vaccine contain?
(iii) Against which diseases do BCG and OPV protect?
(iv) Explain how the vaccine protects the baby.
questions.answer:
(i) The National (Universal) Immunisation Programme.
(ii) A vaccine contains dead or weakened germs (or parts of germs) that cannot cause the disease.
(iii) BCG protects against tuberculosis; OPV (oral polio vaccine) protects against polio.
(iv) The vaccine makes the baby's body produce antibodies and memory cells against the germ, so if the real germ enters later, the immune system destroys it quickly and the baby does not fall ill.
questions.explanation: Immunisation programme; vaccine content; BCG/OPV; mechanism.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A person who had measles as a child does not catch it again, even when classmates have measles.

(i) Which type of immunity protects this person?
(ii) What are the proteins that fight the germ called?
(iii) Why is the response faster the second time?
(iv) How could the same protection have been gained without falling ill?
questions.answer:
(i) Acquired immunity.
(ii) Antibodies.
(iii) After the first infection the body keeps 'memory' cells, so when the same germ appears again antibodies are produced very quickly and the disease is stopped before it develops.
(iv) By vaccination - the measles vaccine produces the same antibodies and memory cells without the person having to suffer the disease.
questions.explanation: Acquired immunity, antibodies, memory, and vaccination as a substitute.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a health camp, three patients are seen: one with bleeding gums, one child with soft bent legs, and one with a swelling in the neck.

(i) Which deficiency disease does each patient most likely have?
(ii) Name the missing nutrient in each case.
(iii) Suggest a food or measure to correct each deficiency.
(iv) Are these diseases communicable?
questions.answer:
(i) Bleeding gums = scurvy; soft bent legs in a child = rickets; swelling in the neck = goitre.
(ii) Scurvy - vitamin C; rickets - vitamin D (and calcium); goitre - iodine.
(iii) Scurvy - citrus fruits like amla, lemon, orange; rickets - sunlight and milk; goitre - iodised salt.
(iv) No. Deficiency diseases are non-communicable - they are caused by a poor diet, not by germs, so they do not spread.
questions.explanation: Diagnose deficiency, name nutrient, suggest food; non-communicable.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A boy is offered a cigarette by his friends, who say it is harmless. Later the same day, a child in the house gets a small burn while cooking.

(i) Name the harmful substance in tobacco and one disease it causes.
(ii) Should the boy accept the cigarette? Give a reason.
(iii) State the correct first aid for the burn.
(iv) Name one thing that should NOT be applied to a burn.
questions.answer:
(i) Tobacco contains NICOTINE; it causes cancer of the mouth and lungs and damages the heart and lungs.
(ii) No. Tobacco is harmful and addictive; he should say no and resist peer pressure to protect his health.
(iii) Cool the burn with clean running water for several minutes and cover it loosely with a clean cloth; seek a doctor if it is serious.
(iv) Ice, oil or toothpaste should NOT be applied to a burn.
questions.explanation: Addiction (tobacco) plus first aid for a burn.
